gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 1 kWh-class LFP power station delivers only about 870–910 Wh at its AC outlets when measured (85–87% of the rated figure), or that small units deliver even less (75–80%). No result states that BLUETTI's own runtime example implies just 76% of rated capacity. ChatGPT used one flat 85% factor for every size.
standout_why: ChatGPT's search returned no results and cited no rival pages, so I compared against its own answer. That answer uses one assumed '85% usable system efficiency' for every size and states no measured per-model output. It also says nothing about how the makers' 'peak', 'surge' and 'Lifting Power' figures differ. OutdoorGearLab's measured table is new to the answer. Its finding that small units lose more (Anker 521 delivered 75%, Anker SOLIX C300 80%) contradicts the flat 85% ChatGPT applied to its smallest '1–2 kWh, Wi-Fi/phones/lights' row.
decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. For a fridge, Wi-Fi and lights, the 1 kWh LFP class delivers 85–87% at the AC outlets when measured, and the models differ by only 2 points: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 890 Wh, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 890 Wh, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 910 Wh from 1,070 Wh, EcoFlow DELTA 3 870 Wh. Usable output therefore shouldn't decide between them. What sizing does change: divide your daily Wh by about 0.85 for a 1 kWh-class unit, but by 0.75–0.80 for a 250–300 Wh unit. BLUETTI's own calculator plans with about 0.76. The fine print also differs: Anker's '3,000 W peak' is a surge rating, while BLUETTI's '2,700 W Lifting Power' is a separate mode (see unsourced), so compare surge figures before planning on a fridge compressor start.

findings.label: Usable AC output vs claimed capacity (OutdoorGearLab measured table)
findings.value: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 890 of 1,024 Wh (87%); Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 890 of 1,024 Wh (87%); DJI Power 1000 V2 880 of 1,024 Wh (86%); EcoFlow DELTA 3 870 of 1,024 Wh (85%); Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 910 of 1,070 Wh (85%); Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 1,710 of 2,042 Wh (84%); Anker SOLIX C300 230 of 288 Wh (80%); Anker 521 192 of 256 Wh (75%)
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab, Best Power Station buying advice, 'Usable AC Power Output' table (Kenji Mowrey, July 13, 2026)
findings.note: Usable % = measured AC Wh ÷ claimed Wh. In this table, units of about 1 kWh and up land at 84–87%. The two units under 300 Wh land at 75–80%.

findings.label: OutdoorGearLab capacity test method
findings.value: AC load of about 80% of each unit's rated maximum, measured at the AC outlets. Across models, usable capacity runs from under 70% to over 90%.
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab, Best Power Station: How We Test (RJ Spurrier, Kenji Mowrey, Sentry Kelly)
findings.note: The load is drawn from a light-bar jig. The page names no instruments and gives no ambient temperature. The losses are attributed mainly to DC-to-AC conversion. A fridge cycling at low average load may convert less efficiently than this 80%-load test; I didn't verify that.

findings.label: Measured AC energy output
findings.value: 910 Wh of 1,070 Wh claimed (85%); 1,500 W max AC output, 3,000 W max AC surge
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 review (Kenji Mowrey, July 23, 2026)
findings.note: This is a reviewer's measurement; the review gives no load details. The 1,500 W continuous and 3,000 W surge figures are also from this review, because Jackery's US product page returned HTTP 429 on three attempts.

findings.label: Maker's runtime example implies a derating factor
findings.value: 200 W load → 3.9 h on BLUETTI's page = 780 Wh = 76% of the rated 1,024 Wh
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,024Wh (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: Arithmetic: 200 W × 3.9 h = 780 Wh; 780 ÷ 1,024 = 0.76. The page footnote: 'Actual runtime may vary depending on power consumption, temperature, battery condition…'. OutdoorGearLab measured 890 Wh (87%) on the same model, so BLUETTI's own estimate is about 11 points more conservative than the measurement.

findings.label: Output, cycle life and price as BLUETTI states them
findings.value: 1,800 W rated AC output; '2,700W Lifting Power'; no surge figure in the Elite 100 V2 spec column; '4,000+ Cycles to 80% Original Capacity'; US$499
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,024Wh (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: The price was also confirmed by storecheck search on bluettipower.com the same day: $499.00, available. In the comparison table, the only 'Surge 2,700W' figure is in the AC180 column, not the Elite 100 V2 column.

findings.label: Output and cycle life as Anker states them
findings.value: 1,024 Wh; 2,000 W continuous AC; 3,000 W peak; 'After 4,000 cycles, the battery still has at least 80% capacity'
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 product page (ankersolix.com)
findings.note: The page showed no US price. Its spec table reads 'L+N+PE', so the page may be a non-US variant. The ×0.85 sizing advice uses OutdoorGearLab's measured 890 Wh (87%) for this model.

findings.label: What 'peak' means across makers (normalisation footnote)
findings.value: Anker gives a '3,000W peak' (surge); BLUETTI gives '2,700W Lifting Power' for the Elite 100 V2 with no separate surge number in its spec column; Jackery gives 3,000 W surge (OutdoorGearLab figure)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Portable Power Station | 1,800W 1,024Wh (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: The Anker figure is from https://www.ankersolix.com/products/c1000-gen2 and the Jackery figure from the OutdoorGearLab review, both read 2026-11-14. The page doesn't say what Lifting Power is; see unsourced.
